name: Tasmanian
confidence_why: Crowley and Dixon 1981 call stress the most elusive part of Tasmanian phonology and conclude only that disyllables are stressed initially and any non-final syllable may bear stress, whereas Taylor 2006 reads the same nineteenth-century diacritics as consistent initial stress and Ritz 1909 as often antepenultimate or freely variable by speaker, so the surviving wordlists do not fix a placement.
catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry & R.M.W. Dixon. 1981. Tasmanian. In R.M.W. Dixon & B.J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, vol. 2, 394-421. Canberra: Australian National University Press.
catalog_locator: §2.4 'Stress', p. 413 (the whole section is on the page headed '2.3 Vowels 413' of the ANU Open Research scan)
catalog_quote: The position of stress within a word is perhaps the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology. We have the following source material: [a] Walker marks each vowel with either ¯ or ˘; these marks apparently indicate accent rather than quantity (see the comment in Roth 1899, p.l of Appendix). [b] Norman uses the same marks, probably in the same way. [c] Milligan says 'when a double consonant or two consonants stand together, the first carries the accent, as in the English words cunningly, peppery, cobbler, pipkin.' This somewhat elusive statement perhaps means that the vowel preceding a sequence of two consonants (in Milligan's orthography) bears stress. [d] Tindale's transcriptions. [e] The Fanny Cochrane Smith recordings. [f] The 1972 Crowley recordings of Mrs. Heffernan and Mrs. Mundy. From these sources it appears that a disyllabic word is always stressed on the first syllable, whereas a trisyllabic word can be stressed on either first or second syllable. Our only general conclusion concerning stress in Tasmanian is thus: any syllable except the last can bear stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Tasmanian languages as a group (reconstructed from 19th-century spellings with accent marks and a few 20th-century recordings): disyllables carry stress on the first syllable; trisyllables on either the first or the second; the final syllable is never stressed. The authors decline to state a fixed rule. (Taylor 2006 reads the same diacritic evidence as regular initial stress; Ritz 1909 as frequent antepenultimate/variable accent.)
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the variability itself; final syllables never stressed; unstressed vowels may reduce to [ə] (p.412).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, inferred from isolated citation forms in wordlists and song recordings; statement is for 'Tasmanian' collectively, with no evidence drawn from South-Western vocabularies.
new_statements.identity_note: The only stress statements found are pan-Tasmanian, not specific to sout3391. Crowley & Dixon 1981 treat 'Tasmanian' (all 15 record-localities) together; their stress evidence (Walker, Norman, Milligan, Tindale, Fanny Cochrane Smith, Crowley's 1972 recordings) comes from eastern/north-eastern/Flinders Island material, and they say of the South-Western and Macquarie Harbour vocabularies that 'the data available.. are so slight that it is bordering on the farcical to draw any inferences from them' (p.403). sout3391 = Bowern 2012's 'southwestern' member of her Western cluster (with Northwestern), created as ISO xpx in 2019; its corpus is essentially G.A. Robinson's west-coast/Port Davey wordlists (in Plomley 1976). No SW-specific phonological analysis exists in anything opened. Any catalog entry should be flagged as a family/areal-level (Tasmanian) statement applied to this languoid.

sources.note: §2.4 Stress, pp.413-414: stress position is 'the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology'; from Walker's/Norman's accent marks, Milligan's remark, Tindale, the Fanny Cochrane Smith cylinders and Crowley's 1972 recordings: disyllables always initial-stressed, trisyllables on first or second; only general conclusion: any syllable except the last can bear stress. Also notes a central vowel [ə] in unstressed syllables (p.412) and that vowel length was probably not phonemic (p.413).

sources.citation: Taylor, John Albert. 2006. The Palawa (Tasmanian Aboriginal) languages: a preliminary discussion. MA thesis, University of Tasmania. doi:10.25959/23206187.v1
sources.note: §7.9 pp.257-259 (and §7.3.3 p.138): disagrees with Crowley & Dixon; argues from the bar/breve diacritics of Walker, Sterling, Robinson, Cunningham that Dixon's 'initial syllable is generally stressed' applies to Palawa words (but not alternating rhythm): 'in 99 per cent of word elements in initial position with vowels bearing these diacritics, the first vowel is marked with a bar' -> 'strong stressing of the first word element in words'. Pan-Palawa, no SW-specific analysis; amateur philological thesis.

sources.citation: Ritz, Hermann B. 1909. The speech of the Tasmanian Aborigines. Papers & Proceedings of the Royal Society of Tasmania 1909: 44-81.
sources.note: pp.48-49: records mark accent by consonant doubling after the accented vowel or a stroke over it; 'the Tasmanian word-accent was quite frequently on the third syllable from the end, the antepenult', but speakers seem 'free to accentuate a word at random or at will' (e.g. languna vs langana 'foot'). Antiquarian, pan-Tasmanian, unreliable.
